strings.name: Mohammed Shia’ al-Sudani
strings.role: Former prime minister of Iraq; leader of the Reconstruction and Development Coalition
strings.summary: Mohammed Shia’ al-Sudani entered national politics through agricultural engineering and local administration in Maysan. He served as human rights minister and labour and social affairs minister before becoming Iraq’s prime minister in 2022. Public services, infrastructure and economic reconstruction were central priorities amid party bargaining and governance challenges. His coalition won the most seats in the 2025 parliamentary election without securing his reappointment. He completed the government handover to his successor, Zaidi, in May 2026.
strings.coverageNote: Sources checked through 18 November 2026; recent activity is supported by meeting reports dated 12 October, 2 November and 12 November. Birthplace and family origins, a lead in parliamentary seats and gaining executive office, and parliamentary approval and swearing-in versus the handover are distinguished. Construction plans and political promises are not treated as completed achievements.
strings.influence.rationale: His premiership and involvement in public services, energy and security policy influence regional stability and economic recovery.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born in Baghdad in 1970 to a family originating from Maysan. He earned a bachelor’s degree in agricultural science at the University of Baghdad in 1992 and worked in agricultural engineering early in his career. Only the corroborated birth year is retained; insufficiently verified master’s or doctoral degrees are not added.
strings.facts.f2.label: From local administration to national politics
strings.facts.f2.value: He joined Maysan’s agriculture administration in 1997, became a local administrator in Amarah in 2004 and served on the provincial council from 2005 to 2009. He subsequently became governor, national minister and member of parliament. These posts are recorded separately from his later premiership.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Infrastructure and economic diversification
strings.highlights.h1.text: His government prioritized roads, electricity and logistics. The Development Road proposal aimed to connect the Gulf, Iraq and Türkiye and reduce dependence on oil revenue. The approximately $17 billion cost and 1,200-kilometre length announced in 2023 were planned figures, not evidence that the entire route was completed or diversification achieved.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Continued political consultation after leaving office
strings.highlights.h2.text: He met Kurdistan Regional Government Prime Minister Masrour Barzani on 12 October 2026, Zaidi on 2 November, and Bafel Talabani and Shaswar Abdulwahid on 12 November to discuss coordination. The meetings show continuing political activity, not his return as prime minister or implementation of the participants’ budget and reform proposals.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Government handover to Zaidi
strings.timeline.t1.text: Ali al-Zaidi received parliamentary approval and was sworn in on 14 May, with 14 ministers approved and other portfolios still pending. The formal Baghdad handover followed on 16 May. Approval, swearing-in and taking over daily duties are recorded separately; al-Sudani was subsequently a former prime minister.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Coalition announces withdrawal of his reappointment bid
strings.timeline.t2.text: A Reconstruction and Development Coalition spokesperson confirmed to Rudaw that the coalition withdrew al-Sudani’s premiership candidacy and backed Maliki to break the formation deadlock. He continued as caretaker prime minister at that point. Maliki did not automatically take office; Zaidi ultimately succeeded him.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Coalition leads the parliamentary election
strings.timeline.t3.text: The Reconstruction and Development Coalition secured 46 of parliament’s 329 seats, with the election commission announcing results on 17 November. Finishing first was insufficient to form a government alone and was not a direct popular election of the prime minister. His bid for a second term still depended on negotiations between parties.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Development Road transport proposal announced
strings.timeline.t4.text: He convened regional transport representatives in Baghdad and presented a rail-and-road scheme linking Iraq’s south and north, the Gulf and Türkiye. Announcement, subsequent financing and construction completion are separate stages; the launch conference did not mean the entire corridor had opened.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Government wins confidence; premiership begins
strings.timeline.t5.text: After a prolonged government-formation deadlock, parliament approved the new government led by al-Sudani, beginning his term as prime minister. The UN subsequently welcomed its formation and called for reform and accountability. Support for forming the government did not mean its governance goals had been fulfilled.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Becomes labour and social affairs minister
strings.timeline.t6.text: In Abadi’s government, he oversaw labour and social protection until 2018. He also held acting responsibilities in finance, trade and industry during this period. Acting appointments, his substantive ministry and their respective terms should not be conflated.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Enters the cabinet as human rights minister
strings.timeline.t7.text: He became human rights minister in Maliki’s second government and remained until 2014. This was leadership of a government department, not an independent human rights organization. The office’s name does not establish that all human rights problems were resolved during his tenure.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Elected governor of Maysan
strings.timeline.t8.text: After serving on the provincial council, he became Maysan’s governor and remained until joining the central government in 2010. The governorship differs from his 2004 local administrative position in Amarah and should not be incorrectly dated to 2005.
